title: Hominin DNA from cave sediments
bodyMd:
Until recently, establishing which hominins had occupied a cave depended on finding their bones, and bones are scarce: a cave may preserve tens of thousands of stone tools and not a single fragment of the people who made them. The recovery of ancient DNA directly from cave sediments promised to break that dependence. Minute quantities of genetic material, shed in skin cells and decaying tissue, bind to mineral grains and can persist for tens of thousands of years, and sequencing sensitive enough to read them needs only a few grams of dirt. Several caves that have never yielded a hominin bone have now yielded hominin DNA.

The promise rests on an assumption: that DNA found in a given layer entered it when that layer formed. Sediment, however, is not inert. Water percolating through a cave floor can carry molecules downward across the boundaries between layers; burrowing animals mix deposits wholesale; later occupants dig pits into earlier floors. Where such processes operate, a sequence taken from a layer dated to sixty thousand years ago may in fact have arrived there much later. Vasquez replies that the objection, though formally correct, is testable rather than fatal: a deposit through which molecules have migrated should betray that movement in its mineralogy and in the vertical distribution of other organic compounds, and in several closely studied caves it does not. Critics answer that the diagnostic signs Vasquez relies on have themselves been calibrated at only a handful of sites.
accessibilityText: A two-paragraph passage about recovering ancient hominin DNA from cave sediments. The first paragraph explains that identifying which hominins used a cave used to require their bones, which are rare, since a cave can hold tens of thousands of stone tools and no human bone fragment at all. It then explains that genetic material shed in skin cells and decaying tissue sticks to mineral grains, survives for tens of thousands of years, and can now be sequenced from only a few grams of sediment, so caves that have produced no hominin bone have produced hominin DNA. The second paragraph states that this depends on the assumption that DNA in a layer arrived when that layer formed, and lists three ways sediment gets disturbed: water carrying molecules downward between layers, burrowing animals mixing deposits, and later occupants digging pits into earlier floors. A researcher named Vasquez argues the objection is testable rather than fatal, because a deposit whose molecules have moved should show that movement in its mineralogy and in how other organic compounds are distributed vertically, and several well-studied caves show no such signs. Critics respond that the diagnostic signs Vasquez uses have been calibrated at only a few sites.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this question bank to fill the missing verbal-reading-comprehension domain. The subject area (sedimentary ancient DNA) is a real field of study, but the wording, the argumentative structure, the researcher name Vasquez, the sixty-thousand-year figure and every specific claim are invented for this item set and are not taken from, or paraphrased from, any ETS passage or any real publication.
